92.title: Migration to Abyssinia
92.hook: a band of persecuted believers flee across the sea to a just Christian king, and Ja'far recites Surah Maryam before him
92.howItsDone: Muslims remember the migration to Abyssinia as the first hijra and honor the Negus as a just ruler; the story is often told as an early example of friendship between Muslims and Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal under the rock on the burning sand. Your line was ahad ahad: One, One. Did you find your one word? Day ninety-two.

The pressure in Mecca keeps rising. The believers who have no powerful family to protect them are being beaten, starved, locked up. And the Prophet ﷺ tells some of them: go. Cross the sea to Abyssinia, in East Africa. There's a king there, he says, under whom no one is wronged. So small groups slip out of Mecca, down to the coast, onto boats, across the Red Sea. Refugees. Families with children. Among them, his own daughter Ruqayyah, and his cousin Ja'far, 'Ali's brother. They land in a Christian kingdom, and for the first time in years, they can pray in peace. Then a delegation from Mecca arrives, carrying expensive gifts for the king.
screen: `NO ONE TO PROTECT THEM.` → `A KING UNDER WHOM NO ONE IS WRONGED.` → `REFUGEES ACROSS THE RED SEA.`

segments.voice: The delegation asks the king, the Najashi, the Negus, to hand the refugees back. Many kings would have taken the gifts. This one says: I won't hand over people who came to me for shelter until I've heard them. The account, told by Umm Salamah, who was there, is preserved in Ibn Ishaq and in the Musnad of Ahmad. The Muslims choose Ja'far to speak. He tells the king: we were a people in ignorance, worshiping idols, cutting family ties, the strong eating up the weak. Then Allah sent us a messenger from among us, whose honesty we knew, and he told us to worship One God, to speak the truth, keep trusts, be good to our relatives and neighbors, and stop harming one another. The king asks: do you have anything of what he brought? And Ja'far recites the opening of Surah Maryam. In Pickthall's words it begins: “A mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah.” Zakariyya's quiet prayer. Maryam. The palm tree. The baby in the cradle. The account says the king wept until his beard was wet, and the bishops around him wept too. And he said: this, and what Isa brought, come from the same source of light. Go in peace; I won't give you up. The delegation went home with their gifts. The Muslims stayed for years. When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ led a funeral prayer for him in Medina, far away, as a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports. Muslims remember him with deep gratitude: a Christian king who protected strangers because it was just.
screen: `HAND THEM BACK, SAYS MECCA.` · `JA'FAR: WHO WE WERE, WHO WE ARE.` · `SURAH MARYAM, AND THE KING WEEPS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE YOU UP.` · then, large: `A JUST KING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who protected a stranger. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone, near or far, who made room for people who weren't their own. A family who took in refugees. A teacher who stood up for the new kid. A doctor, a lawyer, a neighbor. Maybe someone once did it for you or your family. Picture them. Let yourself feel grateful. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them. Then decide how you'll thank them, or someone like them, today. The bell holds the time.
Migration to Abyssinia. The first hijra: persecuted believers crossed the Red Sea and found shelter with a just Christian king.
Your line: a just king. Today, thank one person who protects strangers. Tomorrow, a year of two great losses. Day ninety-two.

93.title: The year of sorrow
93.hook: in one year, he loses both Khadijah and Abu Talib, his wife and his protector
93.carry: grief is a year, not a day
93.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of any death or loss; mourning is marked with prayer, visits and food for the bereaved, and tears are understood as mercy, not weakness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a just king in Abyssinia who wept at Surah Maryam and would not give the refugees up. Your line was a just king. Did you thank someone who protects strangers? Day ninety-three.

Some years take more than one thing from you. The same year the job goes, the parent gets sick. The same winter, two funerals. Anyone who's lived through a year like that knows: the second loss doesn't just add to the first. It lands on a bruise. For the Prophet ﷺ, about ten years after the cave, came a year like that. The Muslims had just come through a long boycott, years when Quraysh refused to trade with his whole clan or marry into it, and families went hungry in a narrow valley. It had finally ended. And then, within a short time of each other, the two people who had held him up all his life died.
screen: `SOME YEARS TAKE TWO THINGS.` → `A LONG BOYCOTT, JUST ENDED.` → `THEN, TWO DEATHS.`

segments.voice: First his uncle, Abu Talib. The man who took him in at eight, raised him, and for ten years of mounting hostility stood between his nephew and Quraysh, because in that society an attack on him meant answering to his clan. Muslims differ on Abu Talib's faith: many Sunni scholars, following a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, hold that he died without accepting Islam, while Shi'a Muslims hold that he was a believer. All remember his protection with honor. And then Khadijah. His wife of twenty-five years. The first to believe. The one who wrapped him in a blanket and said, Allah would never disgrace you. Gone. Muslims call it 'am al-huzn, the Year of Sorrow. And it didn't end with the two funerals. With Abu Talib gone, the protection was gone too, and the insults grew bolder. Ibn Ishaq tells how someone threw dirt on the Prophet's head in the street, and he went home, and one of his daughters washed it off, crying, and he told her: don't cry, my daughter, Allah will protect your father. Notice that nobody is told to hurry past this. The seerah names a whole year after grief. And years later, when the Prophet's baby son Ibrahim died, a hadith in Bukhari says he wept openly and said: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Tears are not a lack of faith. The Qur'an gives words for moments like this, which many Muslims say at every loss: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” And from a surah of this Meccan time: “But lo! with hardship goeth ease.”
screen: `ABU TALIB, HIS PROTECTOR.` · `KHADIJAH, HIS WIFE AND FIRST BELIEVER.` · `'AM AL-HUZN: A YEAR NAMED FOR GRIEF.` · `THE EYES SHED TEARS; THE HEART GRIEVES.` · then, large: `GRIEF IS A YEAR, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a loss that came in pairs. Settle, and breathe. If you've had a season when more than one thing went at once, let it come to mind, gently. You don't have to relive it. Just name both things, quietly. Notice where it sits in your body. Let it be as heavy as it is. If you haven't had a year like that, think of someone who is in one now. If you pray, you can say: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah, and to Him we return. The bell holds the time.
The year of sorrow. 'Am al-huzn: the year he lost both Khadijah and Abu Talib, his wife and his protector.
Your line: grief is a year, not a day. Today, check on someone who lost someone months ago, after the casseroles stopped. Tomorrow, he looks for help in another town. Day ninety-three.

94.title: The road from Ta'if
94.hook: stoned out of Ta'if and bleeding, he is offered revenge, and refuses it
94.tomorrow: the Night Journey and the Hijra
94.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ta'if as the clearest picture of the Prophet's mercy toward those who hurt him, and it is often recalled when Muslims are tempted to answer cruelty with revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the year of sorrow: Khadijah and Abu Talib, both gone. Your line was grief is a year, not a day. Did you check on someone still grieving? Day ninety-four.
screen: `GRIEF IS A YEAR, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: With his protector gone, Mecca is closing in. So the Prophet ﷺ tries somewhere else. He walks, with Zayd, the freed slave he raised as a son, up into the mountains to the town of Ta'if, cooler, greener, a day or two away. He goes to its leaders and asks: will you listen? Will you give me shelter? They don't just say no. They mock him. And as he leaves, they line the road with the town's slaves and its boys, and they throw stones at him. Zayd tries to shield him. By the time they get out, the Prophet's feet are bleeding so much that his sandals are soaked.
screen: `A WALK TO TA'IF.` → `THEY MOCK HIM.` → `STONES, AND BLEEDING FEET.`

segments.voice: Years later, 'Aishah asked him whether any day had been harder than the battle of Uhud. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his answer: yes. That day at Ta'if. He says he walked on, dazed, not knowing where he was, until he looked up and saw a cloud shading him. In it was Jibril, who said: Allah has heard what your people said to you. And with Jibril was the angel of the mountains, who said: if you wish, I will bring the two mountains together and crush them. Think about that. Bleeding, humiliated, with no one left to protect him. And he's offered the one thing a hurt person most wants. Justice. Revenge. The Prophet said no. And then this: I hope that Allah will bring out from their children people who will worship Allah alone. Not them. Their children. He gave up the revenge in exchange for a hope about people not even born yet. On the way home, Ibn Ishaq tells a small moment. Bleeding, he rests in a garden, and a servant named 'Addas brings him some grapes. He says bismillah and eats. 'Addas is surprised: people here don't say that. Where are you from? From Nineveh, 'Addas says. And the Prophet answers: the town of the good man Yunus, son of Matta. He was my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet. The man who walked out on his people in anger, day seventy-five. Here is another prophet, rejected, who doesn't walk away from anyone. And the hope came true. Within a generation, the people of Ta'if became Muslims. The Qur'an says to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.”
screen: `HARDER THAN UHUD.` · `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.` · `GRAPES, AND A MAN FROM NINEVEH.` · `THE HOPE CAME TRUE.` · then, large: `NOT THEM, THEIR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who was cruel. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who hurt you, not the worst person in your life, someone manageable. Notice the part of you that would like them to suffer a little. Don't fight it. Just notice it. Then, if you can, widen the frame: their children, the people who come after them. If you pray, you can ask Allah to guide them, or to bring good from what comes after them. If you don't pray, just wish their children well. The bell holds the time.
The road from Ta'if. Stoned and bleeding, he was offered revenge on the town, and hoped for their children instead.
Your line: not them, their children. Today, when you want someone to pay, try hoping for what comes after them instead. Tomorrow, a night journey, and the road out of Mecca. Day ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 94 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NIGHT JOURNEY AND THE HIJRA.`

95.title: The Night Journey and the Hijra
95.hook: after the night journey and the pledges at 'Aqabah, he slips out of Mecca, hides in a cave, and tells Abu Bakr: do not grieve, Allah is with us
95.howItsDone: Muslims mark the Isra and Mi'raj on the 27th of Rajab in many communities, and the Islamic year begins from the Hijra; 9:40 is often recited for courage in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road from Ta'if: stoned, bleeding, and offered revenge, he hoped for their children instead. Your line was not them their children. Day ninety-five.

After Ta'if, a night. The Qur'an opens its seventeenth surah with it, in Pickthall's words: “Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship.” From Mecca to Jerusalem in one night, the Isra, and then, Muslims say, up through the heavens, the Mi'raj, where the five daily prayers were given. Most scholars say it was a journey of body and soul; some early voices said it was of the spirit. Either way, after the year of sorrow, it came as an honor and a comfort. And then, at the pilgrimage season, a door opens. Men from a town called Yathrib meet him at night at a place called 'Aqabah, and pledge to protect him as they would their own families.
screen: `THE NIGHT JOURNEY.` → `THE FIVE PRAYERS GIVEN.` → `A PLEDGE AT 'AQABAH.`

segments.voice: So the Muslims of Mecca begin to leave for Yathrib, quietly, a few at a time, leaving houses and businesses behind. Quraysh realize what's happening, and the leaders decide: before he can go, kill him. One young man from each clan, so the blame is shared and his family can't take revenge on anyone. The Qur'an mentions their plotting. That night, the Prophet ﷺ asks 'Ali to sleep in his bed, under his green cloak. And he slips out with Abu Bakr. Instead of heading north toward Yathrib, where everyone would look, they go south, and climb to a cave on Mount Thawr. They hide there three nights. Abu Bakr's daughter Asma' brings them food, tearing her waistband in two to tie up the bundles. And the trackers come, right up to the mouth of the cave. Abu Bakr whispers: if one of them looks down at his feet, he'll see us. And the Prophet ﷺ answers, in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: what do you think of two, when Allah is the third? The Qur'an remembers that moment, in Surah At-Tawbah. The Prophet was “the second of two; when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.” People also tell a story of a spider that spun a web across the cave's mouth, and a dove that nested there, so the trackers thought no one could be inside; the Qur'an doesn't mention it, and scholars differ on how reliable the report is. The trackers leave. And the two set out for Yathrib. This leaving is called the hijra: the migration, the breaking away. It is the hinge of Islamic history.
screen: `ONE MAN FROM EACH CLAN.` · `'ALI SLEEPS IN HIS BED.` · `THREE NIGHTS IN THE CAVE OF THAWR.` · `WHAT OF TWO, WHEN ALLAH IS THIRD?` · then, large: `GRIEVE NOT. LO! ALLAH IS WITH US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Find a small, enclosed place, if you can: a closet, a car, the corner of a room, or just cup your hands over your eyes. Make it your cave. Breathe. Let one fear come in with you, something that feels like it's right at the entrance. Then whisper, so quietly only you can hear it. If you pray: Allah is with us. If you don't: I'm not alone in here. Say it a few times, slowly. Then sit, and listen to your own breathing. The bell holds the time.
Hijra. The migration: the Prophet's leaving of Mecca for Yathrib, breaking with the old to begin again.
Your line: Allah is with us. Today, when something scary is at the entrance, whisper your line once before you walk out. Tomorrow, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-five.

screen: `DAY 95 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 2 CLOSE: THE CAMEL KNEELS.`

96.title: Camp 2 close: the camel kneels
96.hook: he reaches Yathrib, where his camel kneels on a plot of land, a mosque is built, and the calendar begins again
96.howItsDone: Muslims date the Islamic year from the Hijra, and many visit the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, which stands on the land where his camel knelt; the first of Muharram marks the Islamic new year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Thawr and the trackers at its mouth. Your line was Allah is with us. Did you whisper it anywhere? Today, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-six.

For days, the people of Yathrib have been walking out to the edge of town every morning, watching the road from Mecca in the heat, and going home disappointed. Then one day a lookout shouts: he's here. The whole town pours out. First he stops at Quba, just outside, and builds a simple mosque there, the first in Islam. Then he rides into the town itself, and everyone wants him. Clan after clan grabs his camel's reins: stay with us, stay with us. And he says, gently: let her go. She is under orders. And the camel, al-Qaswa', walks on through the streets, while the whole town follows her, holding its breath.
screen: `EVERY MORNING, WATCHING THE ROAD.` → `QUBA: THE FIRST MOSQUE.` → `LET HER GO. SHE IS UNDER ORDERS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq and Sahih al-Bukhari both tell where she stopped. The camel knelt on an open yard where dates were laid out to dry. It belonged to two orphan boys. The boys wanted to give it to him as a gift; he insisted on paying them for it. There, with his own hands, carrying bricks alongside everyone else, he built the mosque that still stands at the heart of the city. Yathrib got a new name: Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, or simply al-Madinah, the city. The people who had come from Mecca were the muhajirun, the emigrants. The people of Medina who took them in were the ansar, the helpers. And years later, the Muslims began counting their calendar from this year, six hundred and twenty-two. Not from his birth, not from the cave. From the hijra. The year a community began. And that is where the stories end, for now. Look how far you've come. Seventy-five days ago, on day twenty-two, you met Adam, the steward the angels questioned. Then Iblis who would not bow, and the garden with its one tree. Two sons. Nuh building on dry land. Ibrahim and the idols, the fire made cool, Hajar running between the hills, the House raised. Musa in a basket on the river, the fire on the mountain, the sea. Yusuf, from the well to no blame on you today. Maryam, Zakariyya and Yahya, Isa by Allah's leave. Yunus in three darknesses. And then the Prophet ﷺ himself: an orphan in the desert, a trusted young man, a cave, one word, read, and a road out of Mecca. You know these stories now. Tomorrow, camp three begins: the practices, how Muslims actually pray and live it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list the prophets you now know. Settle, and breathe. Then, slowly, name them to yourself, one per breath. Adam. Nuh. Ibrahim. Isma'il. Musa. Yusuf. Zakariyya. Yahya. Isa. Yunus. Muhammad ﷺ. Add any others you remember. With each name, let one picture come: a boat, a fire, a well, a palm tree, a fish, a cave. If you pray, you can add, peace be upon them. Notice how many you carry now. The bell holds the time.
Camp two, closed. Khalifah, Iblis, waswas, tawbah, khalil, Zamzam, Ka'ba, sabr jamil, nafs, Isa, yatim, amanah, iqra, Hijra: the stories of the prophets, and then the Prophet.
Your line: you know these stories now. Today, tell one of them to someone, in your own words. Tomorrow, camp three opens with the intention behind every prayer. Day ninety-six.

97.title: The intention
97.hook: every prayer begins in the heart, not on the tongue
97.howItsDone: Before each prayer, fast or act of worship, Muslims form an intention in the heart, naming to themselves which prayer or deed it is and that it is for Allah; many schools hold that speaking it aloud is unnecessary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the camel knelt in Medina, and camp two closed with seventy-five days of stories. Your line was you know these stories now. Which one did you tell? Today, camp three: the practices. Day ninety-seven.

Think of two people doing the exact same thing. Both drop a twenty in a charity box. One does it because someone important is watching. The other does it because a kid in the news this morning broke their heart. From the outside, identical. Same twenty, same box. But everyone knows they're not the same. For the next weeks, this path turns from stories to practices, the things Muslims actually do, starting with the prayer, salat, step by step. And the first step isn't a movement or a word. It happens before anything you can see.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, ONE TWENTY, ONE BOX.` → `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.` → `THE FIRST STEP IS INVISIBLE.`

segments.voice: The word is niyyah: intention. What you mean by what you're about to do. The most famous hadith on it is also one of the first in Sahih al-Bukhari; the collection opens with it. The Prophet ﷺ said, in its meaning: actions are only by their intentions, and each person gets only what they intended. Then he gives an example. Two people make the same journey, the hijra from yesterday. One goes for Allah and His messenger. The other goes for money, or to marry someone. Same road. Same dust. Different journeys. So before every prayer, a Muslim forms the intention: this is the noon prayer, four units, for Allah. Where does that happen? Most scholars say in the heart. You don't have to say it out loud; if your heart knows what it's doing, the niyyah is there. Some, especially in the Shafi'i school, recommend saying it quietly as well, to help the heart focus. Either way, it isn't a formula. It's a turning. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. And one more, in Bukhari, is tender: if someone intends a good deed and then can't do it, it is still written for them as a good deed. The intention itself counts. Which means you can make an ordinary day into worship by meaning it. The Qur'an gives words for that: “Lo! my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” Living, too. Not just praying. Mean it first. Everything else follows.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause before starting anything. Before the sit begins, stop. Ask yourself one quiet question: why am I doing this? Not the right answer. The real one. To feel calmer. To learn. To be close to Allah. Because someone I love prays. Let the answer be honest. Then make it on purpose: I'm sitting for this. If you pray, you can make your intention for Allah. Then begin, and when the sit ends, try it once more before the next thing you do. The bell holds the time.
Niyyah. Intention: what you mean by what you do, formed in the heart before every prayer. Camp three's first word.
Your line: mean it first. Today, before three ordinary things, a meal, a meeting, a drive, pause for one breath and decide what you mean by it. Tomorrow, clean body, clean place. Day ninety-seven.

98.title: Clean body, clean place
98.hook: wudu, clean clothes, a clean spot, and the idea behind them
98.howItsDone: Before each prayer, Muslims make sure they are in wudu (the ritual washing of face, arms, head and feet), that their clothes are clean, and that they pray on a clean spot, often a prayer rug; with no water, they use tayammum with clean earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: niyyah, the intention, the prayer that begins in the heart before the tongue. Your line was mean it first. Did you catch yourself pausing before you started something? Day ninety-eight.

Look back at this week for a second. A small band crossing the sea to a just king. A year of grief. A bloody road out of Ta'if. A night journey, a migration, a camel kneeling in Medina. The stories are behind us now, and we've started the practices. Yesterday the prayer began in the heart. Today, before anyone says a word of it, watch what happens at a sink. A man rolls up his sleeves at work, in the restroom, and washes his hands, his mouth, his face, his arms to the elbow, wipes his head, washes his feet. A coworker walks in and looks a little puzzled. He's not being fussy. He's getting ready. Today: the cleanness that comes before the prayer.
screen: `A WEEK OF STORIES, BEHIND US.` → `A SINK AT WORK.` → `HE'S GETTING READY.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is taharah, purity or cleanness. In Islamic law it's the first chapter of almost every book, before prayer, before fasting, before anything, because the prayer isn't valid without it. It has three layers. First, the body. For the daily prayers that usually means wudu, the washing the Qur'an itself describes in Surah al-Ma'idah: wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. After some things, like sleep or using the toilet, the wudu needs to be renewed. After others, like sex, a full bath is needed, called ghusl. Second, the clothes: clean of things like urine or blood. Third, the place: a clean spot to stand on. That's why many Muslims keep a prayer rug. It isn't holy in itself. It's just a clean surface you can carry anywhere. And here's the surprising part. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith in Bukhari, that the whole earth had been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification. A field, a parking lot, the edge of an airport gate. Any clean ground will do. And when there's no water, or water would harm you, there's tayammum: you touch clean earth or dust and wipe your face and hands. The idea behind all of it is in a short hadith in Sahih Muslim: purity is half of faith. Half. Not a rule tacked on to the prayer. Half of the thing itself. Scholars read it as outside and inside together: the water on the skin, and the turning of the heart it's meant to go with.
screen: `TAHARAH — BEFORE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `THE BODY, THE CLOTHES, THE PLACE.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH, A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · `PURITY IS HALF OF FAITH.` · then, large: `OUTSIDE AND INSIDE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one clean corner. Find a spot near you, a corner of the floor, a chair, a patch of desk. Clear it. If you have a clean cloth, a towel or a scarf, lay it down flat and smooth it with your hands. Then sit near it, and just look at it for a moment: a small place where nothing is piled up. Breathe slowly. If you've done wudu before, you can notice where the water would go. If you pray, this is the kind of place you'd pray on. The bell holds the time.
Taharah. Cleanness of body, clothes and place, the half of faith that comes before the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: a clean corner. Somewhere in your day, at home or at work, leave one small corner clearer than you found it. The prayer, step by step, starts here. Day ninety-eight.
